newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Film portrays French Resistance couple.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Film portrays French Resistance couple.

text.p: As ordinary newlyweds, Lucie and Raymond Aubrac joined the Resistance when Germany invaded France in May 1940 and their struggle against the four-year Nazi occupation of France made them national heroes.
More than half a century on, the Aubracs have become the subject of a film by director Claude Berri released in France on February 26.

Called "Lucie Aubrac" and based on her book "Ils Partiront dans l'Ivresse" (They will go in euphoria), the film focuses on the period between May 1943 and February 1944 during which Lucie, pregnant with their second child, risked her life to rescue her husband from jail in the central city of Lyon.

Featuring Daniel Auteil as Raymond and Carole Bouquet, who appears in countless advertisements for Chanel perfumes, as Lucie, the film focuses on the Aubracs' love amid the hazards of occupied France.
FRANCE CONFRONTING WARTIME PAST

The film strikes a chord in France because its release comes at a time when the country is being forced to face its wartime past by the forthcoming trial of former Vichy official Maurice Papon, accused of organising the deportation of 1,560 Jews from the southwestern Bordeaux region.

The Aubracs themselves agreed to endorse the film, in which many of the historical details are modified, only after Berri pledged to donate a generous sum to a foundation devoted to keeping the memory of the Resistance alive.
In the opening scene, Raymond is shown blowing up a train, although he never did.
"The film is well-acted, well-done, moving, whatever you like, but in no way can it be viewed as history," said Henri Amouroux, historian and author of several best-sellers on the Resistance.
Even so, their real life story sounds like a film plot.
Raymond, whose surname was Samuel but who adopted the nom de guerre of Aubrac during the Resistance, was a Jew whose Polish ancestors settled in France in the 18th century.

As head of the armed branch of the left-wing underground movement Liberation, he was arrested by the Gestapo at a meeting of Resistance leaders in the Lyon suburb of Caluire in June 1943, jailed at the Montluc prison and condemned to death.
Determined to free him, Lucie dressed up as the daughter of a wealthy family and went to see Lyon Gestapo chief Klaus Barbie.

Claiming that Claude Ermelin -- the name on Aubrac's false identity papers -- was the father of her unborn child, she asked Barbie for permission to marry him before his death so that she would not suffer the shame of an unmarried mother.
LUCIE NAUSEATED BY LYON GESTAPO BOSS BARBIE

"I was nauseated," Lucie wrote of her meeting with Barbie. "How could I believe that this young man, unremarkable, even a bit vulgar, is the all-powerful master of the city of Lyon? Is it possible that everyone fears this little man?"

Although Barbie refused, Lucie managed to win the consent of another Nazi officer, and as Raymond was being transported back to prison after the marriage, she and a group of Resistance comrades staged a spectacular ambush, killing four German soldiers and freeing Raymond and 14 other prisoners.
Also arrested at Caluire was Jean Moulin, an envoy of exiled Free French leader General Charles de Gaulle who had been entrusted with uniting France's various underground groups.
Long sought by the Gestapo, Moulin was tortured to death by Barbie. His ashes were transferred to the Pantheon, the resting place of France's greatest citizens, in a solemn ceremony in the 1960s.
Although the arrests at Caluire and Raymond's escape are the film's central action, it also briefly touches on the unsolved puzzle of who told the Gestapo of the meeting.
The main suspect, Resistance member Rene Hardy, who attended the meeting although he was not invited and managed to escape, was tried and acquitted twice after the war.
Barbie himself was tracked down in Bolivia in 1983 and extradited to France where he was jailed for life in 1987 for crimes against humanity. He died in prison in 1991.
FILM COINCIDES WITH NATIONAL FRONT VICTORY

The film's release comes in the same month as the extreme-right National Front party's capture of a fourth town hall in municipal elections, raising fears of renewed intolerance of foreigners and minorities. It also coincides with controversy over a tough immigration bill.
The Aubracs, Auteil and Bouquet have all strongly criticised the Front.

Comparing Front members to Hitler during his rage at the victories of black athlete Jesse Owens at the 1936 Olympics, Lucie said during a television interview last week: "They cheat, they lie and they scream, like Hitler screamed."

Lucie returned to teaching after a brief stint in the post-war administration. Raymond worked for the government in Algiers, Marseille and the Ministry for Reconstruction, before devoting himself to work on food aid for the United Nations and developing agriculture projects for developing countries.
At 84, Lucie Aubrac still travels across France to give lectures on the Resistance and tolerance to high schools.
With 10 grandchildren in the family, the Aubracs still seem a perfect couple, united in old age as they were in their fight against Nazi tyranny.
"We were inseparable. Whether it was the Resistance, or his fishing or any decision, we did it together. We were like two halves of a whole," she said in an interview on French radio.
"When one is fortunate enough to have a marriage based not only on the extraordinary physical love we felt for each other but also respect for each others' ideas...it's wonderful."
